query: For a multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its high-temperature solid and liquid states, what single intervention could overcome the limited accuracy, availability, and efficiency of determining melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and liquid thermodynamic properties across a large compositional space? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention and causal mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to current experimental and computational baselines, defines the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes a decisive falsification test against independent reference data.

generation.hypothesis: The single intervention of utilizing machine learning-based molecular dynamics simulations with a carefully curated dataset of high-entropy alloys can overcome the limitations in determining melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and liquid thermodynamic properties across a large compositional space.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its high-temperature solid and liquid states
generation.mechanism: The machine learning algorithm learns patterns in the molecular dynamics simulations, allowing for accurate predictions of thermodynamic properties across various compositions and temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved accuracy, availability, and efficiency in determining melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and liquid thermodynamic properties compared to current experimental and computational baselines
generation.baseline: Current experimental and computational methods for determining thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys
generation.boundary: Applicable to high-entropy alloys with 3-10 principal elements, temperatures between 500-2000 K
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in the accuracy of the machine learning model, potential limitations in the dataset used for training, and the complexity of the high-entropy alloy systems

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of predicted thermodynamic properties from machine learning-based molecular dynamics simulations with independent experimental reference data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted values deviate from the experimental reference data by more than 10%, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems. Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system.
